title: 3 Maccabees
subtitle: a king turned back from the Holy of Holies, and elephants turned against their masters
lead: 3 Maccabees tells how Ptolemy IV Philopator, king of Egypt, after his victory over Antiochus III at Raphia, tried to enter the Holy of Holies in Jerusalem and was struck down when the high priest Simon prayed (1-2), and how he then turned on the Jews of Egypt, who were saved from drunken elephants in the hippodrome of Alexandria when the priest Eleazar prayed (3-7). Despite its name, it has nothing to do with the Maccabees. It has 7 chapters and 228 verses.
facts: The Eastern Orthodox churches read it in their Old Testament. It is not Scripture for the Catholic Church, for Protestants or for Judaism.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, above all of Alexandria.
audience.why: To show that the Most Great God protects his people and his Temple, and that Jews who stay faithful to the Law will be saved, while those who give it up are lost.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern Orthodox churches read 3 Maccabees in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint, as a story of God's care for his people far from Jerusalem.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 3 Maccabees as a Greek story written by an Alexandrian Jew in the late Ptolemaic or early Roman period, using the history of Ptolemy IV freely to speak to the Jews of Egypt about faithfulness, citizenship and God's rescue.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 3 Maccabees is not in the Jewish Bible and left little trace among the rabbis, but it shows how the Jews of Egypt saw themselves: loyal to the king, faithful to the Law, and rescued by God, with a festival of their own.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study the world of the first Christians: Jews of the Diaspora under a pagan ruler, slander and persecution, prayer and rescue by angels, as the early church read such stories.

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers: a Jewish writing outside their Bibles, read for its witness to Jewish faith and life in Egypt before Christ, and tested against the Bible rather than read as the Bible.

canon.summary: 3 Maccabees is read in the Old Testament of the Eastern Orthodox churches. It is not in the Catholic Bible, the Protestant Bible or the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: In the Old Testament, from the Septuagint.

provenance.b: 3 Maccabees was written in Greek, most likely by a Jew of Alexandria.

rejected_why.b: It is not in the Hebrew Bible.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. In progress.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture: the Eastern Orthodox churches.
